look_here_first: Native TEXAS BLUEGRASS is a rhizomatous sod-forming cool-season PERENNIAL, dioecious with male and female plants. Female spikelet florets have conspicuous cobwebby long hairs at basal lemmas that make whole flowering heads look woolly. A distant fuzzy head is only a clue: a verified female floret macro and rooted rhizomes are needed.

best_field_traits: Perennial spreading on underground rhizomes forming prairie grass sod, often 20–70 cm high.
Dioecious: male and female florets on separate individuals.
Female spikelets have strongly woolly/cobwebby basal lemma hair tufts; 20× image essential.
Bright to pale silver flowering heads in spring and smooth sheaths.
Boat-shaped blade tips and a membranous true ligule are genus-level characteristics.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Rooted rhizomatous clump revealing connected new shoots
Female fertile floret 20× macro of cobwebby lemma-base hairs
Male vs female entire panicle from independently identified plants
Ligule and boat-tip macro on intact blade
crew_field_check: Inspect actual rooted base, not only head silhouette.
Boat-shaped leaf tip is shared by Poa species.
Photograph true membranous ligule and mature spikelet/floret details.
Never count Texas bluegrass webby hairs from a blurred landscape view.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Introduced P. annua commonly forms a small shorter-lived tuft with often open triangular green flowering panicles containing bisexual flowers. Texas bluegrass spreads through persistent rhizomes and displays dioecious sex-specific heads; female florets have dense webby hairs at lemma bases. Full panicle color/texture alone is inadequate for ID.
